arXiv:2611.17109v1 [cs.LG] 12 Nov 2026

Near-Optimal Regret for Oracle-Efficient
Adversarial Contextual Bandits

Kiarash Banihashem Affiliation: University of Maryland, College Park Email: kiarash@umd.edu    MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi Affiliation: University of Maryland, College Park Email: hajiagha@umd.edu
Abstract

We study contextual bandits with KK actions, a class of NN policies, and i.i.d. contexts from a distribution that the learner can sample. For any sequence of loss functions fixed before play, we give an oracle-efficient algorithm with expected regret O⁡(K​T​log⁡(2​N)​log⁡(2​K​T))O(\sqrt{KT\log(2N)}\,\log(2KT)) against the best policy in hindsight on the realized contexts. This improves the T2/3T^{2/3} dependence on the horizon in prior oracle-efficient bounds and achieves the optimal regret rate in this setting up to logarithmic factors.

Our algorithm perturbs policy scores using a Poisson sample of auxiliary contexts. At each sampled context, the perturbation assigned to an action is a Laplace noise draw multiplied by a scale specific to that context and action. We show that choosing these scales to minimize a convex objective determined by past observations yields the stated regret bound. We further approximate the minimizing scales by projected stochastic gradient descent using only an exact offline cost-sensitive optimization oracle that returns the optimum value. Since the table of scales can be large, the algorithm represents the SGD iterates implicitly by storing the random draws that determine each update and evaluates the scales only at queried contexts. Both the oracle complexity and the remaining resource bounds are polynomial in TT, KK, and log⁡(2​N)\log(2N).

1 Introduction

In a contextual bandit problem, the learner observes a context on each of TT rounds, chooses one of KK actions, and observes only the loss of that action. Regret is measured against the best policy in hindsight from a class of NN policies. The classical Exp4 algorithm achieves expected regret O⁡(K​T​log⁡N)O(\sqrt{KT\log N}) by maintaining a weight for each policy [2]. When the policy class is large, a natural question is whether one can achieve this rate using only an offline optimization oracle for the class. When contexts and loss vectors are drawn jointly i.i.d., Langford and Zhang [5] obtained a regret bound with T2/3T^{2/3} dependence on the horizon, and Agarwal et al. [1] achieved the optimal square-root rate using an offline optimization oracle.

Achieving square-root regret with an offline optimization oracle becomes much more challenging however when losses are adversarial. In this setting, Rakhlin and Sridharan [7] used auxiliary context samples to obtain expected regret O⁡(T3/4​K1/2​(log⁡N)1/4)O(T^{3/4}K^{1/2}(\log N)^{1/4}). Syrgkanis et al. [8] improved the dependence on the horizon to T2/3T^{2/3}, with regret O⁡((K​T)2/3​(log⁡N)1/3)O((KT)^{2/3}(\log N)^{1/3}). Banihashem et al. [3] then improved the dependence on the number of actions, obtaining O⁡(T2/3​(K​log⁡N)1/3)O(T^{2/3}(K\log N)^{1/3}) regret. More recently, Buzaglo and Hazan [4] obtained O~​(T2/3)\widetilde{O}(T^{2/3}) dependence on the horizon without requiring auxiliary context samples. Despite these advances, achieving the optimal T\sqrt{T} dependence on the horizon with an oracle-efficient algorithm has remained an outstanding open problem.

In this paper, we resolve this problem up to logarithmic factors. We give an oracle-efficient algorithm with expected regret

O⁡(K​T​log⁡(2​N)​log⁡(2​K​T)).O\!\left(\sqrt{KT\log(2N)}\,\log(2KT)\right).

Following prior work, we consider a hybrid setting in which contexts are drawn i.i.d. and the adversary fixes an arbitrary sequence of loss functions before play. The learner can draw independent auxiliary samples from the context distribution. The learner has access to independent samples from the context distribution and to an exact offline oracle that returns the minimum total cost over the policy class. Both the number and the size of the oracle queries are polynomial in TT, KK, and log⁡(2​N)\log(2N) (Theorem 1).

2 Model and Main Result

Let T≥1T\geq 1, K≥2K\geq 2, and let Π\Pi be a nonempty finite class of NN measurable policies π:𝒳→[K]\pi:\mathcal{X}\to[K]. Before play the adversary fixes measurable losses ct:𝒳→[0,1]Kc_{t}:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1]^{K}. The actual contexts xtx_{t} are independent draws from DD. After observing xtx_{t}, the learner chooses qtq_{t}, draws At∼qtA_{t}\sim q_{t} with fresh randomness, and observes only ct​(xt,At)c_{t}(x_{t},A_{t}). Independent auxiliary samples from DD are available. Given a list of contexts and real cost vectors, the value oracle returns

Val⁡((yi,vi)i)=min⁡∑iπ∈Π⁡vi​(π⁡(yi)).\mathrm{Val}((y_{i},v_{i})_{i})=\min_{\pi\in\Pi}\sum_{i}v_{i}(\pi(y_{i})).

We count value-oracle calls, auxiliary context samples, draws from the specified elementary distributions, and exact real-arithmetic operations. The learner is given L=log⁡(2​N)L=\log(2N) or an upper bound L0≥log⁡(2​N)L_{0}\geq\log(2N). Each logarithm and square root used during initialization counts as one exact real-arithmetic operation.

Theorem 1.

Let L=log⁡(2​N)L=\log(2N). Algorithm 2, tuned with LL, satisfies

𝔼​RegT:=𝔼⁡[∑t=1Tct​(xt,At)−min⁡∑t=1Tπ∈Π⁡ct​(xt,π⁡(xt))]≤C​K​T​L​log⁡(2​K​T)\mathbb{E}\mathrm{Reg}_{T}:=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}c_{t}(x_{t},A_{t})-\min_{\pi\in\Pi}\sum_{t=1}^{T}c_{t}(x_{t},\pi(x_{t}))\right]\leq C\sqrt{KTL}\,\log(2KT)

for a universal constant CC. Its number of oracle calls, query sizes, auxiliary context samples, storage and real-arithmetic operations are polynomial in T,K,LT,K,L. A supplied upper bound L0≥LL_{0}\geq L may replace LL in both the tuning and the bounds.

Section 3 reduces regret to a one-round inequality for the ideal action distribution. Section 4 proves its stability estimate. Section 5 implements the distribution to sufficient accuracy to add at most one to the regret bound.

4.1 Information in the inserted context

Lemma 5 (Information carried by one inserted vector).

Fix the score SS and the scale σ\sigma. For each context xx, let C=(M,X1:M)C=(M,X_{1:M}) be the auxiliary pool locations, let Z∼μZ\sim\mu be the independent Laplace vector inserted at xx, and let WxW_{x} be the winning policy in (3).

For each π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, write wπ=Pr⁡(Wx=π∣C)w_{\pi}=\Pr(W_{x}=\pi\mid C). When wπ>0w_{\pi}>0, define the conditional distribution νπ\nu_{\pi} by

νπ​(A)=Pr⁡(Z∈A∣C,Wx=π)for every measurable ​A⊆ℝK.\nu_{\pi}(A)=\Pr(Z\in A\mid C,\,W_{x}=\pi)\qquad\text{for every measurable }A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{K}.

For each action a∈[K]a\in[K], set

Da(x)=𝔼C[∑π∈Π:π⁡(x)=awπ>0wπKL(νπ∥μ)].D_{a}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{C}\!\left[\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\pi\in\Pi:\,\pi(x)=a\\ w_{\pi}>0\end{subarray}}w_{\pi}\,\mathrm{KL}(\nu_{\pi}\|\mu)\right].

Then

𝔼x∼D​[∑a=1KDa​(x)]≤log⁡Nn.\mathbb{E}_{x\sim D}\!\left[\sum_{a=1}^{K}D_{a}(x)\right]\leq\frac{\log N}{n}.
Proof.

For each m≥1m\geq 1, let (X1,Z1),…,(Xm,Zm)(X_{1},Z_{1}),\ldots,(X_{m},Z_{m}) be independent pairs with law D⊗μD\otimes\mu, and define

Wm=arg​maxπ∈Π⁡{S⁡(π)+∑i=1mσπ⁡(Xi)​(Xi)​Zi,π⁡(Xi)},W_{m}=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\pi\in\Pi}\left\{S(\pi)+\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sigma_{\pi(X_{i})}(X_{i})Z_{i,\pi(X_{i})}\right\},

using the same tie-breaking rule as in (3). Write ρm=Pr⁡(M=m)=e−n​nm/m!\rho_{m}=\Pr(M=m)=e^{-n}n^{m}/m!.

n𝔼x∼D[∑a=1KDa(x)]=∑m≥1ρm∑i=1mI(Zi;Wm∣X1:m).n\,\mathbb{E}_{x\sim D}\!\left[\sum_{a=1}^{K}D_{a}(x)\right]=\sum_{m\geq 1}\rho_{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}I(Z_{i};W_{m}\mid X_{1:m}).
Proof of Claim 5.1.

Fix xx and the pool locations CC. Write Ix,C​(Z,Wx)I_{x,C}(Z;W_{x}) for the mutual information under these fixed locations. The inserted vector ZZ has law μ\mu. Conditional on Wx=πW_{x}=\pi, it has law νπ\nu_{\pi}. Thus

Ix,C(Z;Wx)=∑π:wπ>0wπKL(νπ∥μ).I_{x,C}(Z;W_{x})=\sum_{\pi:\,w_{\pi}>0}w_{\pi}\,\mathrm{KL}(\nu_{\pi}\|\mu).

𝔼C​[Ix,C​(Z,Wx)]=∑a=1KDa​(x).\mathbb{E}_{C}[I_{x,C}(Z;W_{x})]=\sum_{a=1}^{K}D_{a}(x).

𝔼x∼D[∑a=1KDa(x)]=∑k≥0ρk𝔼x,X1:k[Ix,(k,X1:k)(Z;Wx)].\mathbb{E}_{x\sim D}\!\left[\sum_{a=1}^{K}D_{a}(x)\right]=\sum_{k\geq 0}\rho_{k}\,\mathbb{E}_{x,X_{1:k}}\!\left[I_{x,(k,X_{1:k})}(Z;W_{x})\right]. (5)

I(Zm;Wm∣X1:m)=I(Zi;Wm∣X1:m),i∈[m].I(Z_{m};W_{m}\mid X_{1:m})=I(Z_{i};W_{m}\mid X_{1:m}),\qquad i\in[m].

mI(Zm;Wm∣X1:m)=∑i=1mI(Zi;Wm∣X1:m),m\,I(Z_{m};W_{m}\mid X_{1:m})=\sum_{i=1}^{m}I(Z_{i};W_{m}\mid X_{1:m}),

which proves the claim. ∎

It remains to bound the inner sum in Claim 5.1. Fix m≥1m\geq 1, write 𝐗=X1:m\mathbf{X}=X_{1:m}, and let Z<i=(Z1,…,Zi−1)Z_{<i}=(Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{i-1}). The noise vectors are independent conditional on 𝐗\mathbf{X}, so I⁡(Zi;Z<i∣𝐗)=0I(Z_{i};Z_{<i}\mid\mathbf{X})=0. For each ii, the chain rule gives

I⁡(Zi;Wm∣𝐗)\displaystyle I(Z_{i};W_{m}\mid\mathbf{X}) ≤I⁡(Zi;Z<i,Wm∣𝐗)\displaystyle\leq I(Z_{i};Z_{<i},W_{m}\mid\mathbf{X})
=I(Zi;Z<i∣𝐗)+I(Zi;Wm∣𝐗,Z<i)\displaystyle=I(Z_{i};Z_{<i}\mid\mathbf{X})+I(Z_{i};W_{m}\mid\mathbf{X},Z_{<i})
=I(Zi;Wm∣𝐗,Z<i).\displaystyle=I(Z_{i};W_{m}\mid\mathbf{X},Z_{<i}).

Summing and applying the chain rule once more yields

∑i=1mI⁡(Zi;Wm∣𝐗)\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{m}I(Z_{i};W_{m}\mid\mathbf{X}) ≤∑i=1mI(Zi;Wm∣𝐗,Z<i)\displaystyle\leq\sum_{i=1}^{m}I(Z_{i};W_{m}\mid\mathbf{X},Z_{<i})
=I(Z1:m;Wm∣𝐗)\displaystyle=I(Z_{1:m};W_{m}\mid\mathbf{X})
≤H⁡(Wm∣𝐗)≤log⁡N,\displaystyle\leq H(W_{m}\mid\mathbf{X})\leq\log N,

since WmW_{m} takes values in the NN-element class Π\Pi. Substituting this bound into Claim 5.1 gives

𝔼x∼D​[∑a=1KDa​(x)]≤1n​∑m≥1ρm​log⁡N≤log⁡Nn.∎\mathbb{E}_{x\sim D}\!\left[\sum_{a=1}^{K}D_{a}(x)\right]\leq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{m\geq 1}\rho_{m}\log N\leq\frac{\log N}{n}.\qed

For each context xx, let g⁡(x)=(π⁡(x))π∈Πg(x)=(\pi(x))_{\pi\in\Pi} denote its prediction signature. ωg=PrX∼D⁡(g⁡(X)=g),Γ+={g:ωg>0}.\omega_{g}=\Pr_{X\sim D}\!\bigl(g(X)=g\bigr),\qquad\Gamma_{+}=\{g:\omega_{g}>0\}.

There is a minimizing scale of the form σa​(x)=sg⁡(x),a∗\sigma_{a}(x)=s^{*}_{g(x),a}, where g⁡(x)=(π⁡(x))π∈Πg(x)=(\pi(x))_{\pi\in\Pi}. The table can be chosen measurably in SS.

Condition on 𝒢=(M,(g⁡(Xi),Zi)i=1M)\mathcal{G}=(M,(g(X_{i}),Z_{i})_{i=1}^{M}). The signature g⁡(Xi)g(X_{i}) determines π⁡(Xi)\pi(X_{i}), and the noise is independent of the contexts. Hence

𝔼⁡[Pπ​(σ)∣𝒢]=∑i=1Msg⁡(Xi),π⁡(Xi)​Zi,π⁡(Xi)=Pπ​(σ¯).\mathbb{E}[P_{\pi}(\sigma)\mid\mathcal{G}]=\sum_{i=1}^{M}s_{g(X_{i}),\pi(X_{i})}Z_{i,\pi(X_{i})}=P_{\pi}(\bar{\sigma}).

Conditional Jensen for the maximum and for u↦log⁡(B/u)u\mapsto\log(B/u) gives

maxπ⁡[S⁡(π)+Pπ​(σ¯)]\displaystyle\max_{\pi}[S(\pi)+P_{\pi}(\bar{\sigma})] ≤𝔼⁡[maxπ⁡[S⁡(π)+Pπ​(σ)]|𝒢],\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\!\left[\max_{\pi}[S(\pi)+P_{\pi}(\sigma)]\,\middle|\,\mathcal{G}\right],

Take expectations in the first line. In the second, multiply by λ​ωg\lambda\omega_{g} and sum over g,ag,a. Adding yields JS​(σ¯)≤JS​(σ)J_{S}(\bar{\sigma})\leq J_{S}(\sigma).

Conversely, every table s∈[1,B]K​|Γ+|s\in[1,B]^{K|\Gamma_{+}|} defines a feasible scale by setting its entries on zero-mass signatures to one. Thus

infσJS​(σ)=infs∈[1,B]K​|Γ+|JS​(s),JS​(s)=F⁡(S,s)+λ​∑g∈Γ+ωg​∑a=1Klog⁡(B/sg,a).\inf_{\sigma}J_{S}(\sigma)=\inf_{s\in[1,B]^{K|\Gamma_{+}|}}J_{S}(s),\qquad J_{S}(s)=F(S,s)+\lambda\sum_{g\in\Gamma_{+}}\omega_{g}\sum_{a=1}^{K}\log(B/s_{g,a}).

The pool term F⁡(S,s)F(S,s) is convex in ss as an expected maximum of affine functions. It is jointly continuous in (S,s)(S,s) since

Use the scale from Lemma 6 in the ideal strategy. For any feasible table ss, let Wx​(s)W_{x}(s) denote the argmax in (3) evaluated at ss, and write

αa(x;s)=𝔼[Za𝟏{Wx(s)(x)=a}].\alpha_{a}(x;s)=\mathbb{E}[Z_{a}\mathbf{1}\{W_{x}(s)(x)=a\}].

Lemma 7 (Derivative of one scale entry).

For g⁡(x)=g∈Γ+g(x)=g\in\Gamma_{+}, the derivative in entry (g,a)(g,a) equals

sg,a∗<B⟹αa​(x)≥λ/(n​sg,a∗).s^{*}_{g,a}<B\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\alpha_{a}(x)\geq\lambda/(ns^{*}_{g,a}). (6)
Proof.

[S⁡(π)+Pπ​(s′)]−[S⁡(π)+Pπ​(s)]=ϵ​∑i=1M𝟏​{g⁡(Xi)=g,π⁡(Xi)=a}​Zi,a.[S(\pi)+P_{\pi}(s^{\prime})]-[S(\pi)+P_{\pi}(s)]=\epsilon\sum_{i=1}^{M}\mathbf{1}\{g(X_{i})=g,\ \pi(X_{i})=a\}\,Z_{i,a}.

Let WmW_{m} be the policy maximizing S​(π)+Pπ​(s)S(\pi)+P_{\pi}(s) for a pool of mm samples, with the fixed tie-breaking rule. We claim that

∂F⁡(S,s)∂sg,a=𝔼⁡[∑i=1M𝟏​{g⁡(Xi)=g,WM​(Xi)=a}​Zi,a].\frac{\partial F(S,s)}{\partial s_{g,a}}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{M}\mathbf{1}\{g(X_{i})=g,\ W_{M}(X_{i})=a\}Z_{i,a}\right]. (7)

∑i=1M𝟏​{g⁡(Xi)=g,π⁡(Xi)=a}​Zi,a.\sum_{i=1}^{M}\mathbf{1}\{g(X_{i})=g,\ \pi(X_{i})=a\}Z_{i,a}.

If two policies differ at XiX_{i}, condition on the locations and all noise coordinates except Zi,π⁡(Xi)Z_{i,\pi(X_{i})}. Since Π\Pi is finite, almost surely all tied maximizers agree at every sampled location and therefore have the same slope. The derivative of the maximum is thus the slope displayed above with π=WM\pi=W_{M}.

Every policy’s absolute slope is at most ∑i=1M|Zi,a|\sum_{i=1}^{M}|Z_{i,a}|. The same bound holds for the absolute difference quotient of the maximum, and its expectation is nn. Dominated convergence therefore gives (7).

where we used n​ωg>0n\omega_{g}>0.

5 Oracle Implementation

Fix the past H=((xi,c^i))i<tH=((x_{i},\hat{c}_{i}))_{i<t} and its score SS. The algorithm uses projected stochastic gradient descent to approximate the minimizer of JSJ_{S}. Its random iterates are functions of a context. A stored list of draws lets us evaluate those functions only where they are needed. After xtx_{t} arrives, independent playouts estimate the winning probabilities at that context.

Theorem 11 (Oracle round).

On each round Algorithm 2 uses polynomial resources in T,K,LT,K,L and satisfies

𝔼⁡[ΦS,xt​(qt)∣ℋt−1]≤𝔼x∼D​ΦS,x​(q∗​(x))+1/T.\mathbb{E}[\Phi_{S,x_{t}}(q_{t})\mid\mathcal{H}_{t-1}]\leq\mathbb{E}_{x\sim D}\Phi_{S,x}(q^{*}(x))+1/T.

Together with Theorem 2 and Lemma 4, this proves Theorem 1. We give the algorithm first and then prove its accuracy and cost.

5.1 Sampling and evaluation

Use n,λ,B,γn,\lambda,B,\gamma from (1). The following choices fix the precision, iteration count, number of probability samples, and pool cap:

δ\displaystyle\delta =1T⁡(1+K/γ),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{T(1+K/\gamma)}, ε\displaystyle\varepsilon =λ​δ232​B2​(n+1),\displaystyle=\frac{\lambda\delta^{2}}{32B^{2}(n+1)}, m\displaystyle m =⌈16​K/δ2⌉,\displaystyle=\lceil 16K/\delta^{2}\rceil,
D0\displaystyle D_{0} =B​K,\displaystyle=B\sqrt{K}, G2\displaystyle G^{2} =K⁡(4​n2+2​λ2),\displaystyle=K(4n^{2}+2\lambda^{2}), J\displaystyle J =max⁡{1,⌈D02​G2/ε2⌉},\displaystyle=\max\{1,\lceil D_{0}^{2}G^{2}/\varepsilon^{2}\rceil\},
η\displaystyle\eta =D0/(G​J),\displaystyle=D_{0}/(G\sqrt{J}), Mmax\displaystyle M_{\max} =⌈(e−1)​n+log⁡(4​(J+m)/δ)⌉.\displaystyle=\left\lceil(e-1)n+\log(4(J+m)/\delta)\right\rceil.

Here D0D_{0} bounds the diameter of the feasible scales, and G2G^{2} bounds the expected squared norm of one stochastic gradient (Lemma 14). A pool UU consists of pairs (Y,Z)(Y,Z) with Y∼DY\sim D, Z∼μZ\sim\mu. Products d⊙Zd\odot Z are coordinatewise. All fresh draws in the algorithms are independent. Write 𝟏\mathbf{1} for the all-ones vector of the required dimension.

Lemma 12 (Replay computes the explicit SGD iterates).

Fix the history HH and the training draws (Uj,Zj)0≤j<J(U_{j},Z^{j})_{0\leq j<J}. Consider explicit projected SGD starting from s0​(y)=𝟏s^{0}(y)=\mathbf{1} and applying the update in Algorithm 4 at every context yy in every step. For each 0≤j≤J0\leq j\leq J and every yy, Algorithm 4 on the first jj records of Algorithm 2 returns

(d,u)=(sj​(y),∑i=0j−1si​(y)).(d,u)=\left(s^{j}(y),\,\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}s^{i}(y)\right).
Proof.

We induct on jj. With no records, replay returns (𝟏,0)=(s0​(y),0)(\mathbf{1},0)=(s^{0}(y),0) for every yy.

Suppose the claim holds after jj records. To build record jj, Algorithm 2 calls replay at each location YY in the new pool UjU_{j}. By induction, the returned scale is sj​(Y)s^{j}(Y). Thus the stored pool is exactly the one explicit SGD constructs:

Pj=[(Y,sj(Y)⊙Z):(Y,Z)∈Uj].P_{j}=\bigl[(Y,s^{j}(Y)\odot Z):(Y,Z)\in U_{j}\bigr].

Now fix any query context yy. After the first jj records, replay has d=sj​(y)d=s^{j}(y). On record jj, replay and explicit SGD therefore compute the same action

Aj​(y)=Winner​(H,Pj,y,sj​(y)⊙Zj).A_{j}(y)=\textsc{Winner}(H,P_{j},y,s^{j}(y)\odot Z^{j}).

For each a∈[K]a\in[K], both update the scale to

saj+1(y)=clip[1,B](saj(y)−η[nZaj𝟏{Aj(y)=a}−λsaj​(y)]).s^{j+1}_{a}(y)=\operatorname{clip}_{[1,B]}\!\left(s^{j}_{a}(y)-\eta\left[nZ_{a}^{j}\mathbf{1}\{A_{j}(y)=a\}-\frac{\lambda}{s^{j}_{a}(y)}\right]\right).

Replay also adds the pre-update value sj​(y)s^{j}(y) to uu, giving u=∑i=0jsi​(y)u=\sum_{i=0}^{j}s^{i}(y). This proves the claim for j+1j+1. ∎

Lemma 13 (Oracle access and cost).

Algorithm 3 returns the winning action in each queried playout almost surely. Per round, Algorithm 2 makes at most

O⁡(K⁡[Mmax​J2+m⁡(Mmax+1)​(J+1)])O\!\left(K\,[M_{\max}J^{2}+m(M_{\max}+1)(J+1)]\right)

value calls, each on at most T+Mmax+1T+M_{\max}+1 contexts.

Proof.

Write Hπ=S⁡(π)+∑(Y,u)∈Puπ⁡(Y)+vπ⁡(y)H_{\pi}=S(\pi)+\sum_{(Y,u)\in P}u_{\pi(Y)}+v_{\pi(y)}. Then

−Va=maxπ[Hπ+𝟏{π(y)=a}],−Va=1+maxπHπ⟺∃π∈arg​maxH:π(y)=a.-V_{a}=\max_{\pi}[H_{\pi}+\mathbf{1}\{\pi(y)=a\}],\quad-V_{a}=1+\max_{\pi}H_{\pi}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \exists\pi\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}H:\pi(y)=a.

Conditional on the other draws, the highest scores of distinct nonempty action groups are constants plus independent continuous shifts sb​(y)​Zbs_{b}(y)Z_{b}. They tie with probability zero. Within a training step this holds jointly for every prediction signature by a finite union: inductively the input scales depend on yy only through its signature. Thus reusing that step at later query locations preserves its winning action almost surely.

Building record jj takes at most j​MmaxjM_{\max} winner calls. Evaluating s¯​(x)\bar{s}(x) costs JJ calls, and each probability trial needs at most J​Mmax+1JM_{\max}+1. Multiplying by KK proves the stated bound. The storage of scaled training records is O⁡(K​J​(Mmax+1))O(KJ(M_{\max}+1)) in addition to the history and working lists. At most (J+m)​Mmax(J+m)M_{\max} auxiliary contexts are drawn. Each list construction and coordinate update costs polynomially many operations in the dimensions shown. A capped count can be sampled with at most Mmax+1M_{\max}+1 independent exponential waiting times of mean one: stop when their sum exceeds nn or Mmax+1M_{\max}+1 arrivals occur by nn. For k≤Mmaxk\leq M_{\max} the probability of kk arrivals is the integral of e−ne^{-n} over 0<t1<⋯<tk<n0<t_{1}<\cdots<t_{k}<n, namely e−n​nk/k!e^{-n}n^{k}/k!. All displayed parameters and the reciprocals of γ,λ,δ,ε\gamma,\lambda,\delta,\varepsilon are polynomially bounded in T,K,LT,K,L since L≥log⁡2L\geq\log 2. ∎

0\displaystyle 0 ≤t⁡(JS​(s)−R⁡(S))−λ2​B2​t​(1−t)​∥s−s∗∥D2,\displaystyle\leq t\bigl(J_{S}(s)-R(S)\bigr)-\frac{\lambda}{2B^{2}}t(1-t)\lVert s-s^{*}\rVert_{D}^{2},

Fix the score vector SS at the start of the round. For a scale ss and a context xx, let pas​(x)p_{a}^{s}(x) be the probability that the winning policy predicts action aa at xx:

pas​(x)=Pr⁡(Wx​(s)​(x)=a).p_{a}^{s}(x)=\Pr\!\left(W_{x}(s)(x)=a\right).

Here SS, ss, and xx are fixed. The probability is over a fresh Poisson pool and an independent noise vector inserted at xx. The scale ss determines the noise multipliers at every pool location and at xx.

Let s∗s^{*} minimize JSJ_{S}. The ideal strategy plays action aa at xx with probability

qa∗​(x)=(1−γ)​pas∗​(x)+γK.q_{a}^{*}(x)=(1-\gamma)p_{a}^{s^{*}}(x)+\frac{\gamma}{K}.

The algorithm instead uses the scale s¯\bar{s} computed by SGD. After receiving xx, it holds s¯\bar{s} and xx fixed and runs mm independent trials, each with a fresh pool and a fresh noise vector at xx. If Ak′A^{\prime}_{k} is the winning policy’s action at xx in trial kk, then the fraction of trials won by action aa and its resulting play probability are

p^a(x)=1m∑k=1m𝟏{Ak′=a},q^a(x)=(1−γ)p^a(x)+γK.\widehat{p}_{a}(x)=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{k=1}^{m}\mathbf{1}\{A^{\prime}_{k}=a\},\qquad\widehat{q}_{a}(x)=(1-\gamma)\widehat{p}_{a}(x)+\frac{\gamma}{K}.
Lemma 15 (Accuracy of the action probabilities before capping).

Suppose the algorithm runs with the pool-size cap disabled. For a fresh context x∼Dx\sim D, its play probabilities satisfy

𝔼⁡[∑a=1K|q^a​(x)−qa∗​(x)|]≤2​B​(n+1)​ε2​λ⏟error from using ​s¯+Km⏟error from estimating win probabilities.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{a=1}^{K}\left|\widehat{q}_{a}(x)-q_{a}^{*}(x)\right|\right]\leq\underbrace{2B\sqrt{\frac{(n+1)\varepsilon}{2\lambda}}}_{\text{error from using }\bar{s}}+\underbrace{\sqrt{\frac{K}{m}}}_{\text{error from estimating win probabilities}}. (11)

The expectation is over the draws used by SGD to compute s¯\bar{s}, the independent context xx, and the mm trials at that context.

Proof.

Fix the incoming score SS and use uncapped Poisson pools.

Claim 15.1.

For any two fixed feasible scales s,ts,t,

𝔼x∼D​∥ps​(x)−pt​(x)∥1≤n+1​∥s−t∥D.\mathbb{E}_{x\sim D}\lVert p^{s}(x)-p^{t}(x)\rVert_{1}\leq\sqrt{n+1}\,\lVert s-t\rVert_{D}.
Proof.

Write X0=xX_{0}=x for the inserted context and X1,…,XMX_{1},\ldots,X_{M} for the ordinary pool contexts. Define QtQ_{t} analogously.

We first compare one coefficient. If V∼Lap⁡(u)V\sim\mathrm{Lap}(u), then 𝔼​|V|=u\mathbb{E}|V|=u, so

KL(Lap(u)∥Lap(v))=𝔼[logvu+|V|(1v−1u)]=log(v/u)+u/v−1≤(u−v)22.\mathrm{KL}(\mathrm{Lap}(u)\|\mathrm{Lap}(v))=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\log\frac{v}{u}+|V|\left(\frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{u}\right)\right]=\log(v/u)+u/v-1\leq\frac{(u-v)^{2}}{2}.

Under QsQ_{s} and QtQ_{t}, the count and locations have the same law. Conditional on them, the coefficients are independent. The chain rule for relative entropy therefore gives

KL(Qs∥Qt)\displaystyle\mathrm{KL}(Q_{s}\|Q_{t}) =𝔼∑i=0M∑a=1KKL(Lap(sa(Xi))∥Lap(ta(Xi)))\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\sum_{i=0}^{M}\sum_{a=1}^{K}\mathrm{KL}\bigl(\mathrm{Lap}(s_{a}(X_{i}))\|\mathrm{Lap}(t_{a}(X_{i}))\bigr)
≤12​𝔼​∑i=0M∑a=1K(sa​(Xi)−ta​(Xi))2\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\sum_{i=0}^{M}\sum_{a=1}^{K}(s_{a}(X_{i})-t_{a}(X_{i}))^{2}
=12​∑k≥0Pr⁡(M=k)​(k+1)​∥s−t∥D2=n+12​∥s−t∥D2.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k\geq 0}\Pr(M=k)(k+1)\lVert s-t\rVert_{D}^{2}=\frac{n+1}{2}\lVert s-t\rVert_{D}^{2}.

Given the locations and coefficients, the same rule under either scale returns (x,A)(x,A): it maximizes S⁡(π)+∑i=0MVi,π⁡(Xi)S(\pi)+\sum_{i=0}^{M}V_{i,\pi(X_{i})} with the fixed tie-breaking order and returns the winner’s action at x=X0x=X_{0}. 𝔼xKL(ps(x)∥pt(x))=KL(Qsx,A∥Qtx,A)≤KL(Qs∥Qt).\mathbb{E}_{x}\mathrm{KL}(p^{s}(x)\|p^{t}(x))=\mathrm{KL}(Q_{s}^{x,A}\|Q_{t}^{x,A})\leq\mathrm{KL}(Q_{s}\|Q_{t}).

𝔼x​∥ps​(x)−pt​(x)∥1≤𝔼x​∥ps​(x)−pt​(x)∥12≤2𝔼xKL(ps(x)∥pt(x))≤n+1​∥s−t∥D.\mathbb{E}_{x}\lVert p^{s}(x)-p^{t}(x)\rVert_{1}\leq\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{x}\lVert p^{s}(x)-p^{t}(x)\rVert_{1}^{2}}\leq\sqrt{2\mathbb{E}_{x}\mathrm{KL}(p^{s}(x)\|p^{t}(x))}\leq\sqrt{n+1}\,\lVert s-t\rVert_{D}.

Claim 15.2.

Conditional on the learned scale s¯\bar{s} and the context xx, the mm fresh trials satisfy

𝔼[∥p^(x)−ps¯(x)∥1|s¯,x]≤K/m.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\lVert\widehat{p}(x)-p^{\bar{s}}(x)\rVert_{1}\,\middle|\,\bar{s},x\right]\leq\sqrt{K/m}.
Proof.

Write pa=pas¯​(x)p_{a}=p_{a}^{\bar{s}}(x). For each aa, the mm indicators 𝟏{Ak′=a}\mathbf{1}\{A^{\prime}_{k}=a\} are conditionally independent Bernoulli variables with mean pap_{a}. Their average p^a​(x)\widehat{p}_{a}(x) therefore satisfies

=Km​(1−∑a=1Kpa2)≤K/m.\displaystyle=\sqrt{\frac{K}{m}\left(1-\sum_{a=1}^{K}p_{a}^{2}\right)}\leq\sqrt{K/m}.

Since x∼Dx\sim D is independent of the training draws, we may apply Claim 15.1 conditional on s¯\bar{s}. Averaging over s¯\bar{s} and using (10) gives

≤Km+2​B​(n+1)​ε2​λ.\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\frac{K}{m}}+2B\sqrt{\frac{(n+1)\varepsilon}{2\lambda}}.

5.3 Regret at the actual score

Lemma 16 (Sensitivity to the played probabilities).

If qa,ra≥γ/Kq_{a},r_{a}\geq\gamma/K for all aa, then |ΦS,x​(q)−ΦS,x​(r)|≤(1+K/γ)​‖q−r‖1|\Phi_{S,x}(q)-\Phi_{S,x}(r)|\leq(1+K/\gamma)\|q-r\|_{1}.

Proof.

Fix SS and xx. For each action aa, write fa(π)=𝟏{π(x)=a}f_{a}(\pi)=\mathbf{1}\{\pi(x)=a\} and define

ga​(b)=R⁡(S)−R⁡(S−b​fa),b≥0.g_{a}(b)=R(S)-R(S-bf_{a}),\qquad b\geq 0.

Thus ga​(b)g_{a}(b) is the decrease in the potential when every policy predicting aa at xx receives a score penalty of bb. We will bound how much the term qa​ga​(ca/qa)q_{a}g_{a}(c_{a}/q_{a}) changes when qaq_{a} is replaced by rar_{a}.

We first verify the properties of gag_{a} used in this bound. Let s0,s1s_{0},s_{1} be minimizing tables at scores S0,S1S_{0},S_{1}, respectively. For 0≤t≤10\leq t\leq 1, put St=(1−t)​S0+t​S1S_{t}=(1-t)S_{0}+tS_{1} and st=(1−t)​s0+t​s1s_{t}=(1-t)s_{0}+ts_{1}. The table sts_{t} is feasible. For every fixed pool, linearity of PπP_{\pi} in the table gives

maxπ⁡[St​(π)+Pπ​(st)]\displaystyle\max_{\pi}[S_{t}(\pi)+P_{\pi}(s_{t})] =maxπ⁡((1−t)​[S0​(π)+Pπ​(s0)]+t⁡[S1​(π)+Pπ​(s1)])\displaystyle=\max_{\pi}\Bigl((1-t)[S_{0}(\pi)+P_{\pi}(s_{0})]+t[S_{1}(\pi)+P_{\pi}(s_{1})]\Bigr)
≤(1−t)​maxπ​[S0​(π)+Pπ​(s0)]+t​maxπ​[S1​(π)+Pπ​(s1)].\displaystyle\leq(1-t)\max_{\pi}[S_{0}(\pi)+P_{\pi}(s_{0})]+t\max_{\pi}[S_{1}(\pi)+P_{\pi}(s_{1})].

Taking expectations and using convexity of the log penalty gives

R⁡(St)≤JSt​(st)≤(1−t)​JS0​(s0)+t​JS1​(s1)=(1−t)​R​(S0)+t​R​(S1).R(S_{t})\leq J_{S_{t}}(s_{t})\leq(1-t)J_{S_{0}}(s_{0})+tJ_{S_{1}}(s_{1})=(1-t)R(S_{0})+tR(S_{1}).

Thus RR is convex. Applying this inequality to the scores S−b0​faS-b_{0}f_{a} and S−b1​faS-b_{1}f_{a} gives

ga​((1−t)​b0+t​b1)\displaystyle g_{a}((1-t)b_{0}+tb_{1}) =R⁡(S)−R⁡((1−t)​(S−b0​fa)+t⁡(S−b1​fa))\displaystyle=R(S)-R\bigl((1-t)(S-b_{0}f_{a})+t(S-b_{1}f_{a})\bigr)
≥(1−t)​ga​(b0)+t​ga​(b1).\displaystyle\geq(1-t)g_{a}(b_{0})+tg_{a}(b_{1}).

The potential is also nondecreasing in each score entry, since increasing a score can only increase the maximum at each fixed table. Adding the same constant to every score shifts every maximum by that constant, so R⁡(S−b​𝟏)=R⁡(S)−bR(S-b\mathbf{1})=R(S)-b. Since 0≤fa≤𝟏0\leq f_{a}\leq\mathbf{1},

R⁡(S)−b=R⁡(S−b​𝟏)≤R⁡(S−b​fa)≤R⁡(S).R(S)-b=R(S-b\mathbf{1})\leq R(S-bf_{a})\leq R(S).

Hence 0≤ga​(b)≤b0\leq g_{a}(b)\leq b and ga​(0)=0g_{a}(0)=0. Moreover, if b0≤b1b_{0}\leq b_{1}, then R⁡(S−b1​fa)≤R⁡(S−b0​fa)R(S-b_{1}f_{a})\leq R(S-b_{0}f_{a}), so ga​(b0)≤ga​(b1)g_{a}(b_{0})\leq g_{a}(b_{1}).

Now fix one action aa and two possible probabilities γ/K≤s≤t\gamma/K\leq s\leq t. Since

cat=st​cas+(1−st)​0,\frac{c_{a}}{t}=\frac{s}{t}\frac{c_{a}}{s}+\left(1-\frac{s}{t}\right)0,

concavity and ga​(0)=0g_{a}(0)=0 give t​ga​(ca/t)≥s​ga​(ca/s)t\,g_{a}(c_{a}/t)\geq s\,g_{a}(c_{a}/s). For the reverse bound on their difference, use ca/t≤ca/sc_{a}/t\leq c_{a}/s and monotonicity of gag_{a}:

0≤t​ga​(ca/t)−s​ga​(ca/s)\displaystyle 0\leq t\,g_{a}(c_{a}/t)-s\,g_{a}(c_{a}/s) =(t−s)​ga​(ca/t)+s⁡(ga​(ca/t)−ga​(ca/s))\displaystyle=(t-s)g_{a}(c_{a}/t)+s\bigl(g_{a}(c_{a}/t)-g_{a}(c_{a}/s)\bigr)

The last inequality uses ca≤1c_{a}\leq 1 and t≥γ/Kt\geq\gamma/K. Taking s=min⁡{qa,ra}s=\min\{q_{a},r_{a}\} and t=max⁡{qa,ra}t=\max\{q_{a},r_{a}\} therefore yields, for every a∈[K]a\in[K],

|qa​ga​(ca/qa)−ra​ga​(ca/ra)|≤Kγ​|qa−ra|.\left|q_{a}g_{a}(c_{a}/q_{a})-r_{a}g_{a}(c_{a}/r_{a})\right|\leq\frac{K}{\gamma}|q_{a}-r_{a}|.

≤∑a=1K|qa−ra|​ca+∑a=1K|qa​ga​(ca/qa)−ra​ga​(ca/ra)|\displaystyle\leq\sum_{a=1}^{K}|q_{a}-r_{a}|c_{a}+\sum_{a=1}^{K}\left|q_{a}g_{a}(c_{a}/q_{a})-r_{a}g_{a}(c_{a}/r_{a})\right|
≤∑a=1K|qa−ra|+Kγ​∑a=1K|qa−ra|\displaystyle\leq\sum_{a=1}^{K}|q_{a}-r_{a}|+\frac{K}{\gamma}\sum_{a=1}^{K}|q_{a}-r_{a}|
=(1+Kγ)​∥q−r∥1.\displaystyle=\left(1+\frac{K}{\gamma}\right)\lVert q-r\rVert_{1}.

Proof of Theorem 11.

Condition on the actual history ℋt−1\mathcal{H}_{t-1}, so the incoming score SS is fixed. Write Prt\Pr_{t} and 𝔼t\mathbb{E}_{t} for probability and expectation conditional on this history. Run the capped and uncapped algorithms with the same context xtx_{t}, pool counts, pool samples, and inserted noise vectors. Let qtq_{t} and q^t\widehat{q}_{t} be their respective play probabilities at xtx_{t}.

Let M1,…,MJ+mM_{1},\ldots,M_{J+m} be the uncapped pool counts and let E={maxiMi>Mmax}E=\{\max_{i}M_{i}>M_{\max}\} be the event that the cap is exceeded. For each Mi∼Poisson⁡(n)M_{i}\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(n),

𝔼t​[eMi]=e−n​∑k=0∞(e​n)kk!=exp⁡((e−1)​n).\mathbb{E}_{t}[e^{M_{i}}]=e^{-n}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(en)^{k}}{k!}=\exp((e-1)n).

By the union bound and Markov’s inequality,

Prt⁡(E)\displaystyle\Pr_{t}(E) ≤∑i=1J+mPrt⁡(eMi>eMmax)\displaystyle\leq\sum_{i=1}^{J+m}\Pr_{t}(e^{M_{i}}>e^{M_{\max}})
≤(J+m)​exp⁡((e−1)​n−Mmax)\displaystyle\leq(J+m)\exp((e-1)n-M_{\max})
≤(J+m)​exp⁡(−log⁡4​(J+m)δ)=δ4.\displaystyle\leq(J+m)\exp\!\left(-\log\frac{4(J+m)}{\delta}\right)=\frac{\delta}{4}.

On EcE^{c}, the two algorithms use exactly the same draws and hence qt=q^tq_{t}=\widehat{q}_{t}. On EE, both outputs are probability vectors, so

∥qt−q^t∥1≤∑a=1K(qt,a+q^t,a)=2.\lVert q_{t}-\widehat{q}_{t}\rVert_{1}\leq\sum_{a=1}^{K}(q_{t,a}+\widehat{q}_{t,a})=2.

Thus the expected error introduced by the cap is

𝔼t​∥qt−q^t∥1=𝔼t​[𝟏​{E}​∥qt−q^t∥1]≤2​Prt⁡(E)≤δ2.\mathbb{E}_{t}\lVert q_{t}-\widehat{q}_{t}\rVert_{1}=\mathbb{E}_{t}\!\left[\mathbf{1}\{E\}\lVert q_{t}-\widehat{q}_{t}\rVert_{1}\right]\leq 2\Pr_{t}(E)\leq\frac{\delta}{2}.

For the uncapped output q^t\widehat{q}_{t}, Lemma 15 applies under the full Poisson law, including draws on which EE occurs. Using ε=λ​δ2/[32​B2​(n+1)]\varepsilon=\lambda\delta^{2}/[32B^{2}(n+1)] and m≥16​K/δ2m\geq 16K/\delta^{2}, we obtain

≤2​B​δ264​B2+δ216=δ2.\displaystyle\leq 2B\sqrt{\frac{\delta^{2}}{64B^{2}}}+\sqrt{\frac{\delta^{2}}{16}}=\frac{\delta}{2}.

Inserting q^t\widehat{q}_{t} between the actual and ideal play probabilities therefore gives

𝔼t​∥qt−q∗​(xt)∥1≤𝔼t​∥qt−q^t∥1+𝔼t​∥q^t−q∗​(xt)∥1≤δ2+δ2=δ.\mathbb{E}_{t}\lVert q_{t}-q^{*}(x_{t})\rVert_{1}\leq\mathbb{E}_{t}\lVert q_{t}-\widehat{q}_{t}\rVert_{1}+\mathbb{E}_{t}\lVert\widehat{q}_{t}-q^{*}(x_{t})\rVert_{1}\leq\frac{\delta}{2}+\frac{\delta}{2}=\delta.

Every coordinate of qtq_{t} and q∗​(xt)q^{*}(x_{t}) is at least γ/K\gamma/K, including on overflow, when qt,a=1/Kq_{t,a}=1/K. Applying Lemma 16 at the same context xtx_{t} gives

𝔼t​[ΦS,xt​(qt)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}[\Phi_{S,x_{t}}(q_{t})] ≤𝔼t​[ΦS,xt​(q∗​(xt))]+(1+Kγ)​𝔼t​∥qt−q∗​(xt)∥1\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{t}[\Phi_{S,x_{t}}(q^{*}(x_{t}))]+\left(1+\frac{K}{\gamma}\right)\mathbb{E}_{t}\lVert q_{t}-q^{*}(x_{t})\rVert_{1}
≤𝔼x∼D​[ΦS,x​(q∗​(x))]+(1+Kγ)​δ\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{x\sim D}[\Phi_{S,x}(q^{*}(x))]+\left(1+\frac{K}{\gamma}\right)\delta

Acknowledgments and AI Usage

This work resulted from extensive interaction between the authors and OpenAI Astra, with the authors providing suggestions and critically checking Astra’s responses through iterative exchanges. OpenAI Astra was also used in writing and revising the manuscript through detailed prompts from the authors, with Gemini Argon assisting in some parts. The authors directed the process and evaluated the proposed ideas and arguments. Lean files formalizing the main theorem are available on https://github.com/kbanihashem/bandit-oracle-lean.

The authors thank Suho Shin and Max Springer for their collaboration on earlier work on this problem, which led to the publication of [3] and Alex Slivkins for originally suggesting the problem.
